title: The bungas
hookLine: the misls built rest-houses round the sacred pool for pilgrims and defenders

lines: A BLANKET ON A BRICK FLOOR.
A FEW STEPS FROM THE WATER.
cards: A blanket unrolled on a brick floor, a few steps from the water. A horse tied up outside.
A rider who has come a long way leaves his things in a room with thick walls and goes down to bathe in the pool and bow at the Harmandir. That room isn't an inn.
Sikh histories say the misls built such houses around the sacred pool, one by one, each put up by a chief or a band. Today's word is what they were called: bunga.

teach.h: A PLACE TO REST BY THE POOL.
teach.b: A bunga did three jobs at once. The first was rest.

Pilgrims coming to the Harmandir needed somewhere to stay, and a bunga gave them a place by the pool, close enough to hear the kirtan, the sung scripture, with no inn to find and no room to bargain for.
The second was defense. In these years the Harmandir had been attacked and damaged, as this path has told, so a bunga was no light guesthouse.
Tradition describes strong buildings, some with high walls, where defenders could stay and keep watch over the pool and the shrine. Rest and guard duty under one roof. The third job was belonging.
Each bunga was tied to a misl, a chief or a community, so riders from that band knew where their place was. A misl miles away the rest of the year had a doorway on the edge of the sacred pool.
Some histories call the building of the Akal Takht itself the Akal Bunga; it faces the Harmandir across the causeway.
The precinct has been rebuilt over the years, and most of the old bungas are gone, though a few still stand.
The idea is worth keeping: around the Harmandir, people built rooms for strangers to rest in.

how: Pilgrims to the Harmandir Sahib today stay in the guest houses (sarais) of the complex, free of charge, and some old bunga buildings still stand near the pool.

games.q: you're a misl chief. your riders come to Amritsar for the gathering and have nowhere to stay near the pool. what do you do?
o: camp out in the fields beyond the city.
build a house by the sacred pool for pilgrims and defenders.
games.why: the misls built bungas around the pool: places to rest, and places to keep watch.

practice: Let your shoulders drop, and bring to mind someone tired right now: a friend with a new baby, a parent working two jobs, someone far from home.
Ask what a bunga would look like for them, a couch for the night, an hour with the kids, a meal they don't have to cook, and settle on one, with Waheguru on each breath out if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Bunga. A rest-house built by a misl or chief beside the sacred pool at Amritsar, for pilgrims to stay and for defenders to keep watch. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bunga, a rest-house or tower-house around the sacred pool.

carryVoice: Your line: rest by the pool. Thick walls, an open door. Until tomorrow.
